title: What New York Decided, and What It Deferred
author: Andrew Marcinek
summary: Andrew Marcinek analyzes New York City's sweeping new AI moratorium, banning student-facing generative AI for roughly 600,000 K-8 students, disabling AI features in 38 previously approved programs, and capping screen time by grade band, arguing the policy gets the easy calls right (companion chatbots have no business counseling a nine-year-old) while dodging the harder equity question underneath it. Drawing on Ken Shelton's LinkedIn critique and UFT president Michael Mulgrew's procurement argument, Marcinek contends the ban simply relocates AI exposure from a supervised school setting to an unsupervised home one, and that relocation is not neutral: children of parents who already use AI professionally get a year of informal, contextualized exposure, while children of parents without that bandwidth get either nothing or unsupervised late-night phone access. He proposes four concrete fixes, procurement-level vendor accountability, K-8 AI literacy rather than a high-school elective, translated guidance sent home, and explicit exit criteria for the moratorium, arguing a ban without preparation just redistributes risk rather than reducing it. The piece closes on the line that protection without preparation leaves students no more empowered than access without purpose.
points: Marcinek's central equity argument is concrete, not abstract: he pictures two seventh graders under the identical ban, one whose parent uses AI at work and models supervised exposure at home, the other left with either nothing or unsupervised phone access after bedtime, both entering ninth grade with the same policy but very different preparation.

He credits the city for admitting institutional failure by disabling 38 previously approved AI-enabled programs, calling it 'a district admitting it had been buying features it never really looked at' rather than framing the moratorium purely as caution.

Ken Shelton's operational questions (what counts as 'using AI' when it's baked into search engines and accessibility tools already; what changes between 8th and 9th grade; who evaluates what stays approved) are foregrounded as the real work every principal now has to do without guidance from the policy itself.

His four concrete recommendations target the policy's design gaps directly: draw compliance responsibility at the vendor/procurement level rather than the individual teacher, make AI literacy a K-8 strand rather than a high-school elective, and require the district to name explicit, measurable exit criteria for when the moratorium ends.
quotes: Companion chatbots have no business offering emotional support to a nine-year-old. AI should not be deciding who graduates, talking a kid through a crisis, or substituting for a teacher's judgment.
When New York says it is disabling 38 programs it had already approved, that is a district admitting it had been buying features it never really looked at.

If AI use simply moves from school to home for a year, this policy does not protect students equally. It protects the ones whose parents already use these tools at work, already have the devices, already have the time and the vocabulary to set limits and explain why.
One has spent a year building judgment. The other has spent a year building habits.
Ken put it in a line I keep rereading: protection without preparation leaves students no more empowered than access without purpose. That is the whole argument.
But a guardrail only tells you where the edge is. It does not teach anyone how to drive. New York has drawn the edge more clearly than any district in the country.
